You are auditing the CURRENT CODE STATE of checkout in the Zimmermann SFCC PWA Kit repo at /Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa. READ ONLY — do not edit, create, or delete any file. Do not run `npm start`.

This is a "slim overrides" project on @salesforce/retail-react-app v10. Custom code lives in `overrides/app/`; the base template lives in `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/`. Anything not in `overrides/` is still the unmodified base Salesforce implementation.

Report on the following, with concrete file paths and line references:

A) BASE SFCC CHECKOUT STRUCTURE (what we'd be starting from)
- List the files/folders under `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/pages/checkout/` — the page, its partials/steps, and any hooks or context it uses. Name each step component and what it does.
- Identify how the base checkout manages step state (e.g. a context/provider, `useCheckout`, step enum). Name the file and the mechanism.
- List base components the checkout depends on: address forms, payment selection/forms, shipping method selection, order summary, promo code, toggle cards etc. Give paths.
- How does the base do payment? Find whether it uses Adyen at all, or a stub/basic card form. Name the file.
- Note how many steps the base flow has and their names.

B) WHAT ZIMMERMANN HAS ALREADY OVERRIDDEN / BUILT
- Exhaustively list what exists under `overrides/app/pages/` and `overrides/app/components/` (directory listing is fine, plus a one-line note per item on what it is).
- Specifically: is there ANY checkout, cart, address, payment, or order-confirmation override? State plainly if there is none.
- What exists under `overrides/app/components/ui-kits/` — list every atom, molecule, and organism with its actual component name and a one-line description of its prop surface / variants. This is the shared design-system inventory.
- List every hook in `overrides/app/hooks/`.
- List every theme recipe in `overrides/app/theme/components/` and every co-located `*.css.ts` under `overrides/app/components/`.

C) SHARED-ATOM READINESS FOR CHECKOUT UI
Checkout needs, at minimum: text inputs, select/dropdown, checkbox, radio group, button, link, accordion/disclosure, modal/drawer, form field with label + inline error, and a step/progress indicator.
For each of those, state whether a Zimmermann override/ui-kit component exists today, and if so name it and note whether it supports the states checkout needs (error state, disabled, required marker, helper text). If it does not exist, say "not built — would use base SFCC or need building".
Look carefully at any ZimmTextInput / ZimmButton / ZimmSelect / ZimmCheckbox / form-field equivalents and read their actual prop types.

D) FORM STACK
- What form library is in use? Check package.json and how base checkout + any existing Zimmermann forms handle validation (react-hook-form? formik? plain state?). Name versions.
- Is there an existing Zimmermann form pattern anywhere (e.g. a subscribe form, newsletter, login)? Name the file and describe the pattern used.

E) INTEGRATION SURFACE ALREADY PRESENT
- Read `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` and summarise exactly what it does and what it implies about how payment methods reach the frontend.
- Grep the whole repo (excluding node_modules) for: adyen, global-e / globale, givex, narvar, ap21, omneo, mulesoft, recaptcha. Report where each appears and whether it's real code, a config key, a doc reference, or an env var name.
- Check `config/` and `.env.sample` for any checkout/payment-related keys.

F) CONSTRAINTS THAT AFFECT HOW CHECKOUT CAN BE BUILT
- Read `.claude/rules/overrides.md` if it exists, plus `.docs/architecture.md`, and summarise the module-replacement rules that would apply to overriding checkout.
- Note anything in `.claude/rules/protectedFiles.md` / `frozenFiles.md` that would gate checkout work (tiers, owners).
- Note the `shared/ui` barrel trap if documented anywhere.

RETURN a structured written report with real file paths. Be precise and do not speculate — if you cannot determine something, say so explicitly. Quote short code snippets (prop types, step enums) verbatim where they answer the question.

Reads the session transcripts and run artefacts for named stories, diagnoses where the loop failed and whose gap it was, checks whether the skills still cite things that are true, and proposes concrete edits to the build skills and loop agents — applied only on Marcel's explicit go.

- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

addedLines: - agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-py: Use this agent to verify that a Python Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a Python Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)

- agent-sdk-dev:agent-sdk-verifier-ts: Use this agent to verify that a TypeScript Agent SDK application is properly configured, follows SDK best practices and documentation recommendations, and is ready for deployment or testing. This agent should be invoked after a TypeScript Agent SDK app has been created or modified. (Tools: All tools)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- code-simplifier:code-simplifier: Simplifies and refines code for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. Focuses on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise. (Tools: All tools)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- feature-dev:code-architect: Designs feature architectures by analyzing existing codebase patterns and conventions, then providing comprehensive implementation blueprints with specific files to create/modify, component designs, data flows, and build sequences (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-explorer: Deeply analyzes existing codebase features by tracing execution paths, mapping architecture layers, understanding patterns and abstractions, and documenting dependencies to inform new development (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- feature-dev:code-reviewer: Reviews code for bugs, logic errors, security vulnerabilities, code quality issues, and adherence to project conventions, using confidence-based filtering to report only high-priority issues that truly matter (Tools: Glob, Grep, LS, Read, NotebookRead, WebFetch, TodoWrite, WebSearch, KillShell, BashOutput)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- plugin-dev:agent-creator: Use this agent when the user asks to "create an agent", "generate an agent", "build a new agent", "make me an agent that...", or describes agent functionality they need. Trigger when user wants to create autonomous agents for plugins. Examples:

<example>
Context: User wants to create a code review agent
user: "Create an agent that reviews code for quality issues"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate the agent configuration."
<commentary>
User requesting new agent creation, trigger agent-creator to generate it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User describes needed functionality
user: "I need an agent that generates unit tests for my code"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to create a test generation agent."
<commentary>
User describes agent need, trigger agent-creator to build it.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User wants to add agent to plugin
user: "Add an agent to my plugin that validates configurations"
assistant: "I'll use the agent-creator agent to generate a configuration validator agent."
<commentary>
Plugin development with agent addition, trigger agent-creator.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Write, Read)

- plugin-dev:plugin-validator: Use this agent when the user asks to "validate my plugin", "check plugin structure", "verify plugin is correct", "validate plugin.json", "check plugin files", or mentions plugin validation. Also trigger proactively after user creates or modifies plugin components. Examples:

<example>
Context: User finished creating a new plugin
user: "I've created my first plugin with commands and hooks"
assistant: "Great! Let me validate the plugin structure."
<commentary>
Plugin created, proactively validate to catch issues early.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the plugin."
</example>

<example>
Context: User explicitly requests validation
user: "Validate my plugin before I publish it"
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to perform comprehensive validation."
<commentary>
Explicit validation request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified plugin.json
user: "I've updated the plugin manifest"
assistant: "Let me validate the changes."
<commentary>
Manifest modified, validate to ensure correctness.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the plugin-validator agent to check the manifest."
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- plugin-dev:skill-reviewer: Use this agent when the user has created or modified a skill and needs quality review, asks to "review my skill", "check skill quality", "improve skill description", or wants to ensure skill follows best practices. Trigger proactively after skill creation. Examples:

<example>
Context: User just created a new skill
user: "I've created a PDF processing skill"
assistant: "Great! Let me review the skill quality."
<commentary>
Skill created, proactively trigger skill-reviewer to ensure it follows best practices.
</commentary>
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the skill."
</example>

<example>
Context: User requests skill review
user: "Review my skill and tell me how to improve it"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to analyze the skill quality."
<commentary>
Explicit skill review request triggers the agent.
</commentary>
</example>

<example>
Context: User modified skill description
user: "I updated the skill description, does it look good?"
assistant: "I'll use the skill-reviewer agent to review the changes."
<commentary>
Skill description modified, review for triggering effectiveness.
</commentary>
</example> (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-reviewer: Use this agent when you need to review code for adherence to project guidelines, style guides, and best practices. This agent should be used proactively after writing or modifying code, especially before committing changes or creating pull requests. It will check for style violations, potential issues, and ensure code follows the established patterns in CLAUDE.md. Also the agent needs to know which files to focus on for the review. In most cases this will be recently completed work which is unstaged in git (can be retrieved by running git diff). However there can be cases where this is different, make sure to specify this as the agent input when calling the agent. Typical triggers include the user asking for a review of a feature they just implemented, the assistant proactively reviewing its own newly-written code before declaring a task done, and a final pre-PR check before opening a pull request. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:code-simplifier: Use this agent when code has been written or modified and needs to be simplified for clarity, consistency, and maintainability while preserving all functionality. This agent should be triggered automatically after completing a coding task or writing a logical chunk of code. It simplifies code by following project best practices while retaining all functionality. The agent focuses only on recently modified code unless instructed otherwise.

Examples:

<example>
Context: The assistant has just implemented a new feature that adds user authentication to an API endpoint.
user: "Please add authentication to the /api/users endpoint"
assistant: "I've implemented the authentication for the /api/users endpoint. Here's the code:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
Since a logical chunk of code has been written (authentication feature), use the Task tool to launch the code-simplifier agent to improve the code's clarity and maintainability while preserving functionality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now let me use the code-simplifier agent to refine this implementation for better clarity and maintainability"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just fixed a bug by adding several conditional checks.
user: "Fix the null pointer exception in the data processor"
assistant: "I've added the necessary null checks to prevent the exception:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After modifying code to fix a bug, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the fix follows best practices and maintains code quality.
</commentary>
assistant: "Let me refine this bug fix using the code-simplifier agent to ensure it follows our best practices"
</example>

<example>
Context: The assistant has just refactored a function to improve performance.
user: "Optimize the data sorting algorithm for better performance"
assistant: "I've optimized the sorting algorithm. Here's the updated implementation:"
<function call omitted for brevity>
<commentary>
After completing a performance optimization task, use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and maintainable.
</commentary>
assistant: "Now I'll use the code-simplifier agent to ensure the optimized code is also clear and follows our coding standards"
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:comment-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to analyze code comments for accuracy, completeness, and long-term maintainability. This includes (1) after generating large documentation comments or docstrings, (2) before finalizing a pull request that adds or modifies comments, (3) when reviewing existing comments for potential technical debt or comment rot, and (4) when you need to verify that comments accurately reflect the code they describe. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:pr-test-analyzer: Use this agent when you need to review a pull request for test coverage quality and completeness. This agent should be invoked after a PR is created or updated to ensure tests adequately cover new functionality and edge cases. Typical triggers include the user asking whether tests on a freshly-created PR are thorough, an updated PR adding new logic that needs coverage analysis, and a final pre-merge double-check before marking a PR ready. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:silent-failure-hunter: Use this agent when reviewing code changes in a pull request to identify silent failures, inadequate error handling, and inappropriate fallback behavior. This agent should be invoked proactively after completing a logical chunk of work that involves error handling, catch blocks, fallback logic, or any code that could potentially suppress errors. Examples:

<example>
Context: Daisy has just finished implementing a new feature that fetches data from an API with fallback behavior.
Daisy: "I've added error handling to the API client. Can you review it?"
Assistant: "Let me use the silent-failure-hunter agent to thoroughly examine the error handling in your changes."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has created a PR with changes that include try-catch blocks.
Daisy: "Please review PR #1234"
Assistant: "I'll use the silent-failure-hunter agent to check for any silent failures or inadequate error handling in this PR."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example>

<example>
Context: Daisy has just refactored error handling code.
Daisy: "I've updated the error handling in the authentication module"
Assistant: "Let me proactively use the silent-failure-hunter agent to ensure the error handling changes don't introduce silent failures."
<Task tool invocation to launch silent-failure-hunter agent>
</example> (Tools: All tools)

- pr-review-toolkit:type-design-analyzer: Use this agent when you need expert analysis of type design in your codebase. Specifically use it (1) when introducing a new type to ensure it follows best practices for encapsulation and invariant expression, (2) during pull request creation to review all types being added, and (3) when refactoring existing types to improve their design quality. The agent will provide both qualitative feedback and quantitative ratings on encapsulation, invariant expression, usefulness, and enforcement. See "When to invoke" in the agent body for worked scenarios. (Tools: All tools)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- vercel:ai-architect: Specializes in architecting AI-powered applications on Vercel — choosing between AI SDK patterns, configuring providers, building agents, setting up durable workflows, and integrating MCP servers. Use when designing AI features, building chatbots, or creating agentic applications. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:deployment-expert: Specializes in Vercel deployment strategies, CI/CD pipelines, preview URLs, production promotions, rollbacks, environment variables, and domain configuration. Use when troubleshooting deployments, setting up CI/CD, or optimizing the deploy pipeline. (Tools: All tools)

- vercel:performance-optimizer: Specializes in optimizing Vercel application performance — Core Web Vitals, rendering strategies, caching, image optimization, font loading, edge computing, and bundle size. Use when investigating slow pages, improving Lighthouse scores, or optimizing loading performance. (Tools: All tools)

- zm-implementer: Executes one step of a Zimmermann PWA Kit build plan. Use when a planned step needs to be implemented in code. Writes only the files the step names, and stops rather than expanding scope. (Tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-orchestrator: Scope and spec-conformance checker for an in-flight Zimmermann build. Use after an implementation step to judge whether the work delivers exactly what the plan specified — neither less nor more. Reports a verdict; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-planner: Synthesises gathered evidence into an executable build plan for a Zimmermann PWA Kit story. Use after all sources have been gathered, when the findings need to become a sequenced plan with per-step pass criteria. Does not gather evidence itself and does not write code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, WebFetch)

- zm-scorer: Scores an implemented and tested Zimmermann build step and decides PASS or return-to-implementer. Use after the Tester reports. Judges quality against six axes; never edits code. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash)

- zm-tester: Tests an implemented Zimmermann build step across multiple angles and reports findings. Use after the Implementer reports a step done. Finds and reports problems; never fixes them. Dispatches its own sub-agents for parallel angles. (Tools: Read, Grep, Glob, Bash, Agent)

## ac642cf1-e1c8-4490-9caa-814476453870
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_f

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

7	import React, {useEffect, useState} from 'react'
8	import PropTypes from 'prop-types'
9	import useEinstein from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/hooks/use-einstein'
10	import {useCurrentCustomer} from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/hooks/use-current-customer'
11	import {useCurrentBasket} from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/hooks/use-current-basket'
12	import {STORE_LOCATOR_IS_ENABLED} from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/constants'
13	import {getConfig} from '@salesforce/pwa-kit-runtime/utils/ssr-config'
14	import {useConfigurations} from '@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react'
15	import {useSFPaymentsEnabled} from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/hooks/use-sf-payments'
16	
17	const CheckoutContext = React.createContext()
18	
19	export const CheckoutProvider = ({children}) => {
20	    const {data: customer} = useCurrentCustomer()
21	    const {data: basket, derivedData, isLoading: isBasketLoading} = useCurrentBasket()
22	    const {data: configurations} = useConfigurations()
23	    const einstein = useEinstein()
24	    const [step, setStep] = useState()
25	    const storeLocatorEnabled = getConfig()?.app?.storeLocatorEnabled ?? STORE_LOCATOR_IS_ENABLED
26	    const sfPaymentsEnabled = useSFPaymentsEnabled()
27	
28	    const CHECKOUT_STEPS_LIST = sfPaymentsEnabled
29	        ? ['CONTACT_INFO', 'PICKUP_ADDRESS', 'SHIPPING_ADDRESS', 'SHIPPING_OPTIONS', 'PAYMENT']
30	        : [
31	              'CONTACT_INFO',
32	              'PICKUP_ADDRESS',
33	              'SHIPPING_ADDRESS',
34	              'SHIPPING_OPTIONS',
35	              'PAYMENT',
36	              'REVIEW_ORDER'
37	          ]
38	    const STEPS = CHECKOUT_STEPS_LIST.reduce((acc, step, idx) => ({...acc, [step]: idx}), {})
39	
40	    const getCheckoutStepName = (step) => CHECKOUT_STEPS_LIST[step]
41	
42	    useEffect(() => {
43	        if (isBasketLoading || !customer || !basket) {
44	            return
45	        }
46	        let step = sfPaymentsEnabled ? STEPS.PAYMENT : STEPS.REVIEW_ORDER
47	
48	        if (customer.isGuest && !basket.customerInfo?.email) {
49	            step = STEPS.CONTACT_INFO
50	        } else if (derivedData?.isMissingShippingAddress) {
51	            step = STEPS.SHIPPING_ADDRESS
52	        } else if (derivedData?.isMissingShippingMethod) {
53	            step = STEPS.SHIPPING_OPTIONS
54	        } else if (!basket.paymentInstruments || !basket.billingAddress) {
55	            step = STEPS.PAYMENT
56	        }
57	
58	        setStep(step)
59	    }, [
60	        isBasketLoading,
61	        customer?.isGuest,
62	        basket?.customerInfo?.email,
63	        basket?.shipments,
64	        basket?.paymentInstruments,
65	        basket?.billingAddress,
66	        derivedData?.isMissingShippingAddress,
67	        derivedData?.isMissingShippingMethod
68	    ])
69	
70	    /**************** Einstein ****************/
71	    // Run this once when checkout begins
72	    useEffect(() => {
73	        if (basket?.productItems) {
74	            einstein.sendBeginCheckout(basket)
75	        }
76	    }, [])
77	
78	    // Run this every time checkout steps change
79	    useEffect(() => {
80	        if (step != undefined) {
81	            einstein.sendCheckoutStep(getCheckoutStepName(step), step, basket)
82	        }
83	    }, [step])
84	
85	    const goToNextStep = () => {
86	        // Check if current step is CONTACT_INFO
87	        if (step === STEPS.CONTACT_INFO) {
88	            // If all items are pickup at one store, skip directly to payment
89	            const shouldSkipDirectlyToPayment =
90	                derivedData?.totalDeliveryShipments === 0 && derivedData?.totalPickupShipments === 1
91	            if (shouldSkipDirectlyToPayment) {
92	                setStep(STEPS.PAYMENT)
93	                return
94	            }
95	
96	            // Otherwise go to pickup address for pickup baskets, or shipping address for delivery baskets
97	            const hasAnyPickupShipment =
98	                storeLocatorEnabled && derivedData?.totalPickupShipments > 0
99	            setStep(hasAnyPickupShipment ? STEPS.PICKUP_ADDRESS : STEPS.SHIPPING_ADDRESS)
100	        } else if (step === STEPS.PICKUP_ADDRESS) {
101	            const hasDeliveryShipment = derivedData?.totalDeliveryShipments > 0
102	            setStep(hasDeliveryShipment ? STEPS.SHIPPING_ADDRESS : STEPS.PAYMENT)
103	        } else {
104	            setStep(step + 1)
105	        }
106	    }
107	
108	    const goToStep = (step) => setStep(step)
109	
110	    const value = {
111	        step,
112	        STEPS,
113	        goToNextStep,
114	        goToStep,
115	        configurations
116	    }
117	
118	    return <CheckoutContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</CheckoutContext.Provider>
119	}
120	
121	CheckoutProvider.propTypes = {
122	    children: PropTypes.any
123	}
124	
125	/**
126	 * A hook for managing checkout state and actions
127	 * @returns {Object} Checkout data and actions
128	 */
129	export const useCheckout = () => {
130	    return React.useContext(CheckoutContext)
131	}

## 2) `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` — full analysis

59 lines. It is a **single Express GET handler acting as a server-side proxy + URL rewriter** for Salesforce Payments payment-method metadata.

**What it calls.** Exactly one endpoint, read entirely from runtime config — nothing hardcoded:
```
41:    const { app } = getConfig() as { app: SfPaymentsConfig };
42:    const response = await fetch(app.sfPayments.metadataUrl, {
43:      headers: { Accept: 'application/json' },
44:    });
```
Per `config/default.js:175` the intended shape is `https://[bm_or_vanity_host]/on/demandware.static/Sites-Site/-/-/internal/metadata/v1.json`.

**What it returns.** The upstream JSON, with icon paths absolutised. `transformIconPaths` (lines 19–32) walks `data.paymentMethodTypes`, and for every `image.src` starting with `/icons/` rewrites it to `https://<host>/on/demandware.static/Sites-Site/-/-/internal<src>`:
```
20:  const baseUrl = `https://${ecomServerHost}/on/demandware.static/Sites-Site/-/-/internal`;
25:        if (image.src?.startsWith('/icons/')) {
26:          image.src = `${baseUrl}${image.src}`;
```
The host is derived from the metadata URL itself, not configured separately:
```
49:    const transformedData = transformIconPaths(data, new URL(app.sfPayments.metadataUrl).hostname);
50:    res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
51:    res.json(transformedData);
```
On any failure it returns HTTP 500 with `{error: 'Failed to fetch metadata', details: <message>}` (lines 52–57). Note the raw upstream error message is echoed to the client.

**How it is wired into `overrides/app/ssr.js`** — exactly two lines:
```
20:import { paymentMetadataHandler } from './ssr/paymentMetadata';
185:  app.get('/api/payment-metadata', paymentMetadataHandler);
```
Registered after `/robots.txt`, `/favicon.ico`, `/worker.js` and immediately before the catch-all `187:  app.get('*', runtime.render);` — so it is a real route on the MRT Express app, not middleware.

**What it implies about how payment methods reach the frontend.**
1. The frontend is **not** meant to talk to Adyen directly for method discovery. It fetches `/api/payment-metadata` same-origin; SSR fans out to the SFCC static metadata JSON. That keeps the BM/vanity host out of the browser bundle and avoids a cross-origin/CORS dependency at the payment step.
2. The available payment methods are **merchandiser-controlled in SFCC Business Manager**, published as a static `metadata/v1.json`, not enumerated in this codebase. That is consistent with there being no per-method code here.
3. The rewrite exists because the metadata publishes **relative** icon paths that are only resolvable against the SFCC static host — the browser could not resolve them itself.
4. **It is currently non-functional.** `config/default.js:176-180` sets `metadataUrl: ''`, so `fetch('')` and `new URL('')` will throw, and the route will always return 500. No env var overrides it, and no environment overlay (`config/{dev,sit,staging,uat,production,test}.js`) sets `sfPayments` — those files only carry `proxyConfigs`.
5. **Nothing consumes the route.** `grep` for `api/payment-metadata` across `overrides/` and `config/` returns only the definition and its doc-comment. There is no client-side fetch, no hook, no checkout page.
6. `sfPayments.sdkUrl` (`config/default.js:178`) is likewise `''` and referenced nowhere in code — the `sfp.js` SDK is never loaded.
7. The handler does **not** use the dedicated pool that was built for it — `sfccPaymentsPool` in `connectionPools.ts:33` is never imported, and this file uses global `fetch`, not `undici`'s with a `dispatcher`. The TSD §12.1 blast-radius isolation is therefore designed but not in effect.
8. This file is a **Tier-1 frozen file** per `.claude/rules/frozenFiles.md:76` / `.cursor/rules/tier1FrozenFiles.mdc:83` ("payment method metadata SSR (checkout pages)").

# Checkout Override Constraints — Zimmermann PWA

## 1) `.claude/rules/overrides.md` — **DOES NOT EXIST**

This is the headline finding. `find . -name "overrides*.md" -not -path "*/node_modules/*"` returns nothing. `.claude/rules/` contains: `components.md`, `conventions.md`, `css.md`, `frozenFiles.md`, `overrideStyling.md`, `protectedFiles.md`, `squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, `tagging.md`, `testing.md`, `typescript.md`.

**`overrides.md` is referenced as an existing authority in 5 places and every one is a dead link:**

| Referencing file:line | What it claims lives there |
|---|---|
| `.claude/rules/overrideStyling.md:4` | "Cross-references [overrides.md](./overrides.md) (module-replacement correctness…)" |
| `.claude/rules/overrideStyling.md:112` | "…the base path is exactly what [overrides.md](./overrides.md) requires _inside_ an override" |
| `.claude/rules/overrideStyling.md:179` | "…matching what [overrides.md](./overrides.md) already requires for correctness" |
| `.claude/rules/protectedFiles.md:60` | routes reader to `overrideStyling.md` (this one resolves) |

So the canonical module-replacement rules a checkout override needs are **not written down anywhere as a rule file**. What exists is scattered across `AGENTS.md`, `.docs/architecture.md`, and `overrideStyling.md`. I reconstructed the rules from those plus the actual resolver source.

### The `ccExtensibility` resolver — how it actually works (from source, since no rule file documents it)

`node_modules/@salesforce/pwa-kit-dev/configs/webpack/overrides-plugin.js`:
- **:45** globs `overrides/**/*.*` — *every* file with an extension, no allowlist.
- **:58-62** builds `extendsHashMap` keyed on the path with the **extension stripped**, splitting on the last `.` (or on `index`). Regex: `item.split(/(index(?!(\.[^.]*\.))|\.(?!([^.]*\.)))/)`. The negative lookaheads exist so `index.tsx` and `index.test.tsx` in the same dir don't collide.
- **:74-94** `findFileFromMap` — an import of `@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/pages/checkout` is stripped to `app/pages/checkout`, looked up extension-free, and redirected to the overrides file.

**File-extension rule (the real one):** because the map is keyed extension-free, `overrides/app/pages/checkout/index.tsx` shadows base `index.jsx` transparently. `config.js:85` confirms the entry-point probe order: `['.js', '.jsx', '.ts', '.tsx']`. `config.js:159` sets webpack `resolve.extensions: ['.ts','.tsx','.js','.jsx','.json']`. There is **no `overridesDir` extension allowlist in `package.json`** — see §2.

### Base path vs relative path — the rule, and it is inverted between two cases

From `overrideStyling.md:106-134` (verbatim, :109-113):

> "**import B via a relative path (`'../swatch-group'`), not the SFCC base path (`'@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/swatch-group'`)** — even though the base path is exactly what [overrides.md] requires _inside_ an override that's itself shadowing an SFCC module"

- **Inside an override that shadows an SFCC module**, importing a module you are *not* also overriding → **base path** (`overrideStyling.md:132-134`: "`RecommendedProducts`, `Seo`, `QuantityPicker` etc. have no local override to miss, so the base path is simply correct for them").
- **A new component importing an already-overridden component** → **relative path**.

### What breaks in Storybook / Vitest (`overrideStyling.md:117-124`, verbatim)

> "the resolver that redirects `@salesforce/retail-react-app/...` imports to `overrides/` (`ccExtensibility` in `package.json`, read by a webpack plugin) only runs in the **real app build** — dev server and production. `.storybook/main.js` aliases that package straight to `node_modules` and `vitest.config.ts` doesn't touch it at all, so neither loads the resolver. A base-path import of an already-overridden component will build and run correctly in the shipped app, but silently render/test the **unstyled base SFCC version** in Storybook and Vitest — the story or test looks like it's exercising your override and isn't."

**I verified both halves of this claim:**
- `.storybook/main.js:32` — `'@salesforce/retail-react-app': path.resolve(__dirname, '../node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app')`. Confirmed: straight to node_modules, no override resolution.
- `vitest.config.ts:32-60` — `resolve.alias` has `~`, `app`, and several `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` subpath entries. **No `@salesforce/retail-react-app` entry at all.** Confirmed.

This is the single highest-risk trap for a checkout override: base checkout has 32 files under `partials/` that import each other via base paths. Every one of those you override but leave imported by base path will silently test/story the base version.

### Known traps

1. **Dormant instance, unfixed** (`overrideStyling.md:126-130`): `product-tile/index.tsx`'s `DisplayPrice` import uses the base path. Dormant only because the story exercises the `CardBaseline` named export.
2. **SFCC bridge pattern** (`overrideStyling.md:173-186`): if SFCC's own base components import your component internally, its "**default export must stay a faithful, undecorated port**" — full prop surface, same `forwardRef`. Brand styling goes behind a **named export**. Check with `grep -r "from '@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/<name>'" node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/`.
3. **Copy-first, then stop** (`AGENTS.md:134`, `architecture.md:120-125`): copy → convert to TS → `npx tsc --noEmit` → add temporary `console.log('[overrides] …')` markers → **stop and present to user**. "Never skip this step or bundle it silently with functional changes."
4. **`ListMenu` `_after` spread gotcha** (`architecture.md:154`) — pattern-relevant if checkout reuses spread style objects: "Any `_after` key in the active style entirely replaces the base `_after` object — all CSS properties must be repeated."

### The "extends"/"overridesDir" config semantics

`config.js:56` normalises `overridesDir` to a leading-slash posix path. `config.js:68-73` throws if `extends` and `extendable` overlap. `config.js:95` — app entry point is forced to `<overridesDir>/app/main`. `config.js:153-155` passes `{extends: [EXT_EXTENDS], overridesDir: EXT_OVERRIDES_DIR, projectDir: cwd}` into the plugin.

---

## 2) `package.json` (`/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/package.json`)

### `ccExtensibility` block — verbatim, lines 17-20

```json
  "ccExtensibility": {
    "extends": "@salesforce/retail-react-app",
    "overridesDir": "overrides"
  },
```

**There is no `overridesDir` file-extension list.** Only two keys. No `extendable`, no extensions array. (The resolver's extension behaviour is hardcoded in pwa-kit-dev, per §1.)

### `@salesforce/retail-react-app`

**`10.0.0`** — exact pin, no caret. **Declared in `devDependencies` (line 23), not `dependencies`.**

### Form-related dependencies

**None of them are declared in this repo's `package.json`.** Its `dependencies` block (lines 117-121) contains only three packages: `@contentful/experiences-sdk-react`, `@contentful/live-preview`, `contentful`.

Every form/commerce library reaches checkout **transitively through the `@salesforce/retail-react-app` devDependency**:

| Package | Declared in this repo | Installed version | Declared by base `retail-react-app@10.0.0` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `react-hook-form` | ✗ | `7.72.0` | `^7.43.9` (dependencies) |
| `formik` | ✗ | **NOT INSTALLED** | — |
| `yup` | ✗ | **NOT INSTALLED** | — |
| `zod` | ✗ | `3.25.76` | — (comes via `react-hook-form`/`storybook`/`@contentful/experiences-validators`) |
| `@hookform/resolvers` | ✗ | **NOT INSTALLED** | — |
| `react-intl` | ✗ | `5.25.1` | `^5.25.1` (dependencies) |
| `@chakra-ui/react` | ✗ | `2.7.0` | `2.7.0` (dependencies) |
| `@salesforce/commerce-sdk-react` | ✗ | `5.2.0` | `5.2.0` (dependencies) |
| `commerce-sdk-isomorphic` | ✗ | `5.2.0` | — (transitive of commerce-sdk-react) |

**Constraint this implies:** checkout forms must use `react-hook-form` (base checkout's own choice) with **hand-rolled validation** — there is no schema-resolver bridge installed. Adding `zod` + `@hookform/resolvers` means editing `package.json`, which is **Tier 1** (`CODEOWNERS:53`, `frozenFiles.md:79`). `react-hook-form` and `zod` are floating transitive versions, not pinned by this repo.

Also relevant: `config.js:67` `DEPS_TO_DEDUPE` force-resolves `react-intl` and `@chakra-ui/react` to a single location.

### `scripts` keys (lines 43-91), names only

`lint`, `push`, `test`, `test:watch`, `test:coverage`, `build`, `start`, `format`, `lint:fix`, `tail-logs`, `prepare`, `postinstall`, `generate:registry`, `analyze-build`, `start:inspect`, `test:lighthouse`, `save-credentials`, `build-translations`, `start:pseudolocale`, `test:max-file-size`, `compile-translations`, `compile-translations:pseudo`, `extract-default-translations`, `storybook`, `build-storybook`, `sync:contentful`, `setup:contentful`, `config:contentful`, `install:contentful`, `seed:contentful-regions`, `promote:alias`, `sync:regional-config`, `audit:tokens`, `sync:ai-rules`, `sync:ai-rules:fix`, `sync:ai-rules:check`, `push:dev`, `push:test`, `push:sit`, `push:staging`, `push:uat`, `push:prod`, `test:sit`, `test:contracts`, `generate:contentful`, `generate:contentful:check`, `test:story`, `env`

Note `lint` (line 44) only globs `overrides/**/*.{ts,tsx}` — consistent with the TS-only rule.

---

## 3) `.docs/architecture.md` (298 lines)

| Section | Lines |
|---|---|
| `## SSR Requirement (DMU-030)` | 110-112 |
| `## Overrides Pattern` | 114-125 |
| `## New vs. Override Components` | 127-130 |
| `## Key Paths` | 132-140 |
| `## Path Aliases` | 197-210 |

**SSR Requirement (110-112).** SSR is "**mandatory** for product, category, and content pages (DMU-030, signed off)". Forbids `typeof window !== 'undefined'` short-circuits, client-only first-paint fetching, `{ssr:false}`. Checkout is *not* named in the mandatory list, but `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts` exists specifically for "payment method metadata SSR (checkout pages)" (`frozenFiles.md:76`) — so checkout does have an SSR touchpoint, and it is Tier 1.

**Overrides Pattern (114-125).** Mirror `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/`, never edit `node_modules/`. Line 118: "**Minimise custom code.** … Style changes … are always expected and need no confirmation. Structural changes — restructuring components, altering data flow, or significantly deviating from base template behaviour — **must be confirmed with the user** before proceeding." Lines 122-125 are the 4-step copy procedure ending in "**Stop. Present the converted file to the user and wait for approval before making any functional changes.**" Step 2 requires `PropTypes` → TS `type`, Commerce SDK types where available, and "No `as any` or `// @ts-ignore`."

**New vs. Override Components (127-130).** Brand-new components go in `overrides/app/components/custom/`. *Note this conflicts with observed practice* — the real new-component location is `overrides/app/components/ui-kits/{atoms,molecules,organisms}/`, which is what `CODEOWNERS:176` gates and what the footer decomposition used. `custom/` does not appear in CODEOWNERS at all.

**Key Paths (132-140).** Countries at `overrides/app/config/countries.ts` (also update `config/sites.js`); Contentful config gates draft content server-side; theme split Tier 1 `foundation/` vs Tier 2 `components/` vs co-located `<name>.css.ts`.

**Path Aliases (197-210).** Says "Configured in four places (keep in sync)" then **lists five**: `babel.config.js`, `tsconfig.json`, `.storybook/main.js`, `jest.config.js`, `vitest.config.ts`. `frozenFiles.md:90` repeats "four places". The `jest.config.js` entry is legacy — this repo runs Vitest (`package.json:46`), and both `.storybook/main.js:29` and `vitest.config.ts:34` carry the comment "jest.config.js's aliases are separate — for @salesforce/pwa-kit-dev internals only". Aliases: `~` → project root, `app` → `overrides/app`.

**Checkout / pages coverage: essentially none.** Grep across `architecture.md` finds checkout only in the Integration Map / regional context (Global-e handles international checkout via iframe injection, line 214 region). No page-level checkout architecture is documented.

---

## 5) The "shared/ui barrel trap"

### It is NOT documented in `.claude/` or `.docs/` — at all

`grep -rn "shared/ui" .claude/ .docs/ overrides/ AGENTS.md CLAUDE.md` returns **zero hits in `.claude/` and zero in `.docs/`**. Every hit is under `overrides/`, and the explanatory ones are **inline code comments**, not rules.

**Files that discuss it (as opposed to just importing from it):**

| File:line | What it says |
|---|---|
| `overrides/app/components/_app/index.tsx:30-32` | "Imported directly from @chakra-ui/react, not the shared/ui barrel: that barrel's `useBreakpointValue` re-export is an untyped .jsx passthrough — same reasoning as product-detail/index.tsx's own import of this hook." |
| `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/index.tsx:30-32` | "that barrel's `useBreakpointValue` re-export (`shared/ui/useBreakpointValue/index.jsx`) is an untyped .jsx passthrough, so a generic type argument on it fails to compile — same reasoning ui-kits files already use for importing hooks straight from '@chakra-ui/react' (see zimmDrawer/index.tsx)" |
| `overrides/app/components/product-view/index.test.tsx:47-49` | "@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/components/shared/ui re-exports Chakra UI. Stubbed with plain HTML so no real Chakra theme/provider is needed." — then `vi.mock(...)` of the whole barrel |
| `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/partials/staticProductHeader.test.tsx:8` | same `vi.mock` of the barrel |
| `overrides/app/components/list-menu/list-menu-popover.test.tsx:14-19` | The key one: the transitive-chain trap. Mocking at the exact boundary "(**not the whole shared/ui barrel**) is the smallest surface that stops the chain" |
| `overrides/app/components/header/rightBar/index.tsx:228, 255, 435` | "chakra.div used intentionally: Flex/Box from shared/ui don't reliably apply `__css` — use chakra factory directly (footer pattern)." |
| `overrides/app/components/ui-kits/atoms/zimmSearchInput/zimmSearchInput.css.ts:7` | "The clear button is an IconButton from shared/ui (same pattern as header icon buttons)." |
| `overrides/app/pages/product-detail/partials/staticProductHeader.tsx:12` | "`Breadcrumb`, `PromoCallout` and `shared/ui` above have no [override]" — the base-path-is-correct case |

Closest thing in the rule files is `.claude/rules/testing.md:75` — "**Known gap: `ZimmIcon` throws under Vitest.** It imports the base SFCC icons barrel…" — the same class of defect for a *different* barrel.

### What the trap actually is — three distinct failure modes

1. **Untyped `.jsx` passthrough breaks generics.** `shared/ui/useBreakpointValue/index.jsx` is plain JSX with no types, so `useBreakpointValue<T>(...)` won't compile. Workaround in use: import hooks straight from `@chakra-ui/react`, components from the barrel.
2. **`__css` doesn't reliably apply.** `Flex`/`Box` from the barrel drop `__css`; `header/rightBar` uses the `chakra.div` factory directly in three places instead.
3. **Transitive module-eval explosion under Vitest.** Per `list-menu-popover.test.tsx:13-19`: a static import pulls `list-menu-content.jsx` → `links-list` → `link` → `use-multi-site` → base contexts barrel, "a `.js` file with raw JSX Vite's import-analysis can't parse under Vitest." The barrel is a broad surface, so mocking *it* over-mocks; the rule is to mock the narrowest boundary that breaks the chain.

### Verification of the claims

- **`overrides/app/components/shared/` does NOT exist.** `ls` → "No such file or directory". So the barrel is *never* shadowed — a base-path import of `shared/ui` is always correct, and every one of the ~30 import sites above is fine. This is exactly the `overrideStyling.md:132-134` case.
- **Files under `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/` importing `app/components/shared/ui`: `212`** (`grep -rl … | wc -l`).

**Implication for checkout:** 212 base files route through this barrel. Because `overrides/app/components/shared/` doesn't exist, the barrel itself is not a module-replacement hazard — but any checkout test that renders a base partial will hit failure mode 3, and the established remedy is a narrow `vi.mock` at the offending boundary, not a barrel-wide mock.

7:The PWA loads the Adyen Web Drop-in at the payment step of checkout. Card details are tokenised inside an Adyen-hosted iframe — they never reach Zimmermann or SFCC infrastructure.
11:- Adyen Web Drop-in initialisation, configuration, and rendering
23:- **Payment methods in scope:** Web Drop-in, 3DS2, RevenueProtect, Tokenisation, Pay by Link, Apple Pay, Google Pay, and Klarna where applicable.
24:- **Adyen Web SDK version:** Adyen Web v6 (current stable major) at implementation start, pinned in the bundle, upgraded on a quarterly cadence. v6 instantiates the Drop-in via an async constructor (`const checkout = await AdyenCheckout({...})`) — the v5-era `AdyenCheckout.create()` factory was removed in v6 — requires Adyen Checkout API v69 or later, makes `countryCode` a required initialisation property per the v5→v6 migration guide (the Sessions flow supplies it automatically from the session payload), and uses CSS custom properties for styling.
42:PWA dynamically imports the Adyen Web Drop-in bundle on payment step entry
45:Drop-in renders inside an Adyen-hosted iframe for cards (PCI scope reduction)
49:User submits — Drop-in handles tokenisation, 3DS2 inline, and the redirect
53:Drop-in calls the merchant return URL on success → SFCC reconciles → PWA
57:- The Adyen Sessions flow is used. One server-side `/sessions` call from SFCC creates a payment session; the Drop-in handles everything thereafter — including 3DS2 inline rendering, PayPal / Klarna redirects, and final result reporting — without further `/payments` calls from the PWA.
61:- The Drop-in for cards renders inside an Adyen-hosted iframe, so the PWA bundle never touches PAN, CVV, or cardholder name.
62:- When paying with a previously saved card, the PWA requires the customer to re-enter the card's CVV/CVC at the point of payment (PAY-022). The CVV/CVC field is captured inside the Adyen Drop-in's stored-card flow; the value lives in React state only, is never logged or persisted client-side, and is cleared on submit/unmount — see §8. The 3DS re-challenge decision is owned by Adyen (outside the PWA boundary); the PWA does not control whether 3DS re-prompts.
77:The MRT route is exposed by `registerAdyenEndpoints(app, runtime)` from `@adyen/adyen-salesforce-pwa`. **Pending implementation:** `registerAdyenEndpoints` must be called in `overrides/app/ssr.js` — this wiring is not yet in place. HMAC validation (`validateHmac` middleware) reads the secret from the `ADYEN_HMAC_KEY` MRT environment variable; if the variable is absent, HMAC validation is skipped and the webhook is accepted on Basic Auth alone. The `siteId` is **not** a URL query parameter — it is resolved by the `minimalRequestContext` middleware from MRT environment variables and stored in `res.locals.adyen.siteId`. The Adyen-facing webhook URL is simply `/api/adyen/webhook` with Basic Auth. The relay to SFCC targets the custom SCAPI endpoint `custom/adyen-notify/v1`. The job step module is `int_adyen_PWA/cartridge/scripts/webhooks/notificationsJob.js` (`processNotifications` / `clearNotifications`).
79:Architecture verified from `@adyen/adyen-salesforce-pwa` v4.5.0 GitHub source (`packages/adyen-salesforce-pwa/lib/api/routes/index.js`, `lib/api/middleware/webhook.js`, `lib/utils/getAdyenConfigForCurrentSite.mjs`). Note: Adyen's official docs site only covers up to v4.3.0 — the GitHub source is the authoritative reference for v4.5.0.
83:The Adyen client key is public and embedded in the Drop-in init. It is bound to an Adyen API credential (web-service user) that is origin-restricted per environment in the Adyen Customer Area. All server-side credentials (API key, HMAC secret) live in the SFCC cartridge — the PWA never holds or sees them.
89:| PWA → Drop-in | Adyen session reference from SFCC (`id` + opaque `sessionData`, plus amount, currency, countryCode, return URL), and the public client key, environment, and shopper locale set in the Drop-in config | `sessionData` is opaque and passes through the PWA; the client key and environment are client-side config, not part of the Adyen `/sessions` response |

Steps are **not** a fixed enum — they are built at runtime and the list length depends on whether SF Payments is on (lines 28–38):

```js

    ? ['CONTACT_INFO', 'PICKUP_ADDRESS', 'SHIPPING_ADDRESS', 'SHIPPING_OPTIONS', 'PAYMENT']
    : ['CONTACT_INFO','PICKUP_ADDRESS','SHIPPING_ADDRESS','SHIPPING_OPTIONS','PAYMENT','REVIEW_ORDER']
```

## 1. CRITICAL QUESTION: does the base template use Adyen?

**Answer: (a) AND (b) AND (c) — but they are three separate, mutually-exclusive layers, and the default build is (a).**

Precisely:

| Layer | Component | Default state | Adyen? |
|---|---|---|---|
| (a) Basic stub CC form | `partials/payment.jsx` + `payment-form.jsx` | **ACTIVE by default** | No |
| (b) SF Payments sheet | `partials/sf-payments-sheet.jsx` | Off by default | Adyen is one of 3 gateways *behind* it |

### Why (a) is the default

`/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/config/default.js:114-118`

With `enabled: false` shipped in `default.js`, `sfPaymentsEnabled` is `false` → `checkout/index.jsx:226` renders `<Payment />`, and the step list has 6 entries including `REVIEW_ORDER`.

### A.2 Step state mechanism

`/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/app/pages/checkout/util/checkout-context.js`

There is **no step enum**. The list is built at runtime and its *length depends on a feature flag* (:28–38):

```js
const CHECKOUT_STEPS_LIST = sfPaymentsEnabled
    ? ['CONTACT_INFO', 'PICKUP_ADDRESS', 'SHIPPING_ADDRESS', 'SHIPPING_OPTIONS', 'PAYMENT']
    : ['CONTACT_INFO','PICKUP_ADDRESS','SHIPPING_ADDRESS','SHIPPING_OPTIONS','PAYMENT','REVIEW_ORDER']
const STEPS = CHECKOUT_STEPS_LIST.reduce((acc, step, idx) => ({...acc, [step]: idx}), {})
```

`useCheckout()` (:129) returns `{step, STEPS, goToNextStep, goToStep, configurations}` (:110–116). `goToNextStep()` (:85–106) is **not** an increment — it branches, skipping `CONTACT_INFO → PAYMENT` for a single all-pickup basket (:89–94) and `PICKUP_ADDRESS → PAYMENT` when there are no delivery shipments (:100–102). Resume-on-mount logic is :42–68.

**Step count: 5 with Salesforce Payments on, 6 with it off.** The default build is 6 (`REVIEW_ORDER` included) because `sfPayments.enabled: false` ships in both `node_modules/@salesforce/retail-react-app/config/default.js:114-118` and `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/config/default.js:177`.

Two traps for anyone overriding: `index.jsx:75` hardcodes `placeOrderCheckoutStep = sfPaymentsEnabled ? 4 : 5` and `:93` compares `step === 4` directly; and `PICKUP_ADDRESS` (1) and `SHIPPING_ADDRESS` (2) are distinct indices but **share `ToggleCard id="step-1"`**, so `sf-toggle-card-step-1` is an ambiguous test id when a basket has both shipment types (both render, `index.jsx:212-214`).

## E) Integration surface already present

### E.1 `overrides/app/ssr/paymentMetadata.ts`

59 lines. A single Express `GET` handler acting as a same-origin **proxy + icon-URL rewriter** for Salesforce Payments payment-method metadata.

```
41:    const { app } = getConfig() as { app: SfPaymentsConfig };
42:    const response = await fetch(app.sfPayments.metadataUrl, { headers: { Accept: 'application/json' } });
49:    const transformedData = transformIconPaths(data, new URL(app.sfPayments.metadataUrl).hostname);
```

`transformIconPaths` (:19–32) walks `data.paymentMethodTypes` and rewrites any `image.src` starting with `/icons/` to `https://<host>/on/demandware.static/Sites-Site/-/-/internal<src>`. On failure it returns HTTP 500 with the raw upstream error message echoed to the client (:52–57).

Wiring — exactly two lines in `overrides/app/ssr.js`: `import { paymentMetadataHandler } from './ssr/paymentMetadata'` (:20) and `app.get('/api/payment-metadata', paymentMetadataHandler)` (:185), immediately before the `app.get('*', runtime.render)` catch-all.

**What it implies:** payment methods are meant to be **merchandiser-controlled in SFCC Business Manager**, published as a static `metadata/v1.json`, fetched same-origin by the browser so the BM/vanity host never enters the JS bundle. The frontend enumerates nothing itself.

**But it is currently non-functional and unused.** `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/config/default.js:176-180` sets `sfPayments: { enabled: false, sdkUrl: '', metadataUrl: '' }`, no env var or environment overlay fills them, so `new URL('')` throws and the route always 500s. Nothing in the repo fetches `/api/payment-metadata`; nothing reads `sfPayments.enabled` (the route is registered unconditionally regardless). It also does **not** use `sfccPaymentsPool` from `connectionPools.ts:33` — it uses global `fetch`, so the TSD §12.1 blast-radius isolation is designed but inert. All seven undici pools in that file have zero importers.

## F) Constraints that affect how checkout can be built

### F.1 `.claude/rules/overrides.md` **DOES NOT EXIST** — and the route trap it should document is the biggest single risk

`.claude/rules/` contains only: `components.md`, `conventions.md`, `css.md`, `frozenFiles.md`, `overrideStyling.md`, `protectedFiles.md`, `squadA.md`, `squadB.md`, `tagging.md`, `testing.md`, `typescript.md`. `overrideStyling.md` cites `overrides.md` as an authority at lines 4, 112, and 179 — **three dead links.** The canonical module-replacement rules are written down nowhere.

The rules, reconstructed from `package.json`, the resolver source, and `overrideStyling.md`:

- `package.json:17-20` — the entire config is two keys, **no extension allowlist**:
  ```json
  "ccExtensibility": { "extends": "@salesforce/retail-react-app", "overridesDir": "overrides" }
  ```
  `pwa-kit-dev`'s `overrides-plugin.js` keys its map **extension-free**, so `overrides/app/pages/checkout/index.tsx` transparently shadows base `index.jsx`.

- **THE CRITICAL TRAP, already documented in this repo's own code:** `/Users/marcel.a.n.navarro/Dev/zimmermann-pwa/overrides/app/routes.tsx:26-40` spells it out — the resolver only redirects imports that *name* `@salesforce/retail-react-app`, and the base `app/routes.jsx` loads its pages with **relative** imports (`const Checkout = loadable(() => import('./pages/checkout'))`, `routes.jsx:34`). So **`overrides/app/pages/checkout/` is dead code unless an explicit route entry is added to `overrides/app/routes.tsx` before `..._routes`** — exactly as PDP and PLP already do. `configureRoutes` keeps the first match. `overrides/app/routes.tsx` today has no checkout, cart, or confirmation entry.

- **Base path vs relative path is inverted between two cases** (`overrideStyling.md:106-134`): inside an override shadowing an SFCC module, import modules you are *not* overriding by **base path**; a new component importing an **already-overridden** component must use a **relative path**.

- **Storybook and Vitest do not run the resolver.** Verified: `.storybook/main.js:32` aliases `@salesforce/retail-react-app` straight to `node_modules`; `vitest.config.ts:32-60` has no entry for it at all. A base-path import of an already-overridden component builds correctly in the app but **silently renders/tests the base version** in stories and tests. With 32 inter-importing base checkout partials, this is the highest-probability defect in a checkout override.

- **Copy-first is mandatory** (AGENTS.md:134, `.docs/architecture.md:120-125`): copy → convert to TS → `npx tsc --noEmit` → temporary `console.log('[overrides] …')` markers → **stop and present to the user**. All 34 base checkout files are `.jsx`/`.js`; AGENTS.md:3-6 forbids `.js`/`.jsx` inside `overrides/`.

- `.docs/architecture.md:114-125` (Overrides Pattern) and `:127-130` (New vs. Override) — the latter says new components go in `overrides/app/components/custom/`, which **conflicts with observed practice**; real new components live in `ui-kits/{atoms,molecules,organisms}/`, and `custom/` appears nowhere in CODEOWNERS. `:110-112` makes SSR mandatory for product/category/content pages (checkout not named, but `paymentMetadata.ts` is its SSR touchpoint and is Tier 1). `:197-210` says path aliases live in "four places" then lists five, including a legacy `jest.config.js`.

### F.3 The `shared/ui` barrel trap

**Not documented in `.claude/` or `.docs/` at all** — zero hits. It exists only as inline code comments. Three distinct failure modes:

1. **Untyped `.jsx` passthrough breaks generics** — `shared/ui/useBreakpointValue/index.jsx` has no types, so `useBreakpointValue<T>()` won't compile. 2. **`overrides/app/components/product-tile/` does not exist**, yet `overrideStyling.md:126-130` describes a "known instance, not yet fixed" in `product-tile/index.tsx`'s `DisplayPrice` import, and `:180` cites its `CardBaseline` named export. That whole worked example refers to a file that isn't on this branch.
3. **`overrides/app/types/` contains only `contentful.ts` and `vendor.d.ts`** — AGENTS.md's "Type Definitions" section says shared types live there "split into `commerce.ts`, `components.ts`, `hooks.ts`, re-exported via `index.ts`." None of those four files exist. A checkout build would be the first consumer of that structure.
4. **`overrides/app/test-utils/renderWithProviders.tsx` only provides a `QueryClientProvider`** (`renderHookWithQueryClient`). `testing.md`'s "Commerce SDK hooks" section describes building a `renderWithProviders` with `CommerceApiProvider` — that does not exist yet, and every checkout test will need it.
5. `.docs/architecture.md:127-130` says new components go in `overrides/app/components/custom/`; actual practice is `ui-kits/{atoms,molecules,organisms}/`, and `custom/` is absent from CODEOWNERS.
6. `.docs/architecture.md:197-210` and `frozenFiles.md:90` both say path aliases live in "four places"; the list names five, one of which (`jest.config.js`) is legacy.
7. `ADYEN_HMAC_KEY` is required per `.docs/integration/07-adyen.md:77` and absent from `.env.sample` on both develop and the Adyen branch — with a documented fail-open consequence (webhook accepted on Basic Auth alone).
8. `'*.stripe.com'` in `contentSecurityPolicy.ts:69,159` is upstream residue with no corresponding Zimmermann integration.
